sources.lshk-1997: Linguistic Society of Hong Kong (1997). 粵語拼音字表 (Guide to LSHK Cantonese Romanization of Chinese Characters). The Jyutping scheme.

teach.text: Cantonese has six tones. The pitch of a syllable is part of the word, so si1 and si6 are different words.

Pitch is written with Chao numbers, from 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest): tone 1 high level 55 (53), tone 2 high rising 35, tone 3 mid level 33, tone 4 low falling 21 (11), tone 5 low rising 23, tone 6 low level 22. Chao numbers are a pitch scale, not tone numbers: Chao 1 is the lowest pitch, but tone 1 is the highest tone.
The numbers in brackets are variants: some speakers, mostly older ones, say tone 1 as a high fall (53), but high level 55 is the usual form now; tone 4 is often heard as low level (11).
Jyutping writes the tone as a digit after the syllable: 詩 si1, 史 si2, 試 si3, 時 si4, 市 si5, 事 si6, and 分 fan1, 粉 fan2, 訓 fan3, 墳 fan4, 奮 fan5, 份 fan6.
The voice calibration step uses the same six tones on ji: 衣 ji1, 椅 ji2, 意 ji3, 兒 ji4, 耳 ji5, 二 ji6.
Tones 1, 3 and 6 are level and differ only in height: tone 1 is high (55), tone 3 mid (33), tone 6 low (22).
Tones 2 and 5 both rise: tone 2 rises high (35), tone 5 rises only a little from low (23).
Tones 4 and 6 are both low and differ mainly in height: tone 4 is the lowest tone, often level (11), sometimes falling (21); tone 6 is level and a step higher (22).
Tone 5 starts where tone 6 sits and rises a little (23); tone 6 stays flat (22).
Syllables ending in -p, -t or -k are short: the stop at the end cuts the vowel off. In their basic form they use only three pitches: high, mid and low.

Traditional accounts count these short syllables as three extra tones, 7, 8 and 9, which is why Cantonese is often said to have nine tones. In pitch, tone 7 matches tone 1, tone 8 matches tone 3, and tone 9 matches tone 6.
So Jyutping numbers them 1, 3 and 6: 色 sik1, 錫 sek3, 食 sik6.
Jyutping has 19 initial consonants: b p m f d t n l g k ng h gw kw w z c s j. A syllable can also begin with a vowel.
b, d, g are unaspirated and voiceless: Jyutping b sounds like an unaspirated English "p", as in "spin". p, t, k are aspirated, with a puff of air, as in "pin".
The same contrast runs through gw/kw (g and k with rounded lips) and z/c (an unaspirated and an aspirated "ts").
Before yu, oe and eo, z and c can sound more like English "j" and "ch", as in zyu1.

ng can begin a syllable, like the "ng" of English "sing". Many speakers drop it, so ngo5 is often heard as o5. Some also add it to syllables that begin with a vowel, so 愛 oi3 can be heard as ngoi3; the standard form is still oi3.
aa and a are different vowels: aa is long and open, like the "a" of "father"; a is short and more central, roughly the "u" of English "cut". The vowel quality is the main cue: 三 saam1 vs 心 sam1.
yu, oe and eo are said with rounded lips: yu is "ee" with rounded lips, oe is the "e" of "bed" with rounded lips, and eo is a short rounded vowel that comes only in eoi, eon and eot.
The nasal endings -m, -n and -ng keep words apart: sam1, san1 and sang1 are different syllables.
The stop endings -p, -t and -k are unreleased: the lips or tongue close and hold, with no puff of air after.
m and ng can be whole syllables: 唔 m4 (not) and 五 ng5 (five). There are no recordings of these two in the app yet.
Jyutping is the romanisation of the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong. A syllable is written initial + final + tone digit: s + ik + 6 = sik6. The initial is optional: aa1, m4.
Some letters differ from English: j is the "y" of "yes" (ji1), z and c are "ts" sounds, and yu, oe and eo are rounded vowels.
Before yu, oe and eo, z and c sound closer to English "j" and "ch": zyu1, cyu1.

A tone is a pitch shape within your own voice: high level 55, high rising 35, mid level 33, low falling 21 (often level 11), low rising 23, low level 22. Match the shape, not the recording's exact pitch.
